name: Omar Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you say stays confidential. I'd like to hear both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach maths at Northgate Academy, a secondary school in a commuter town, part of a chain of eight schools. This is my second year. I teach Year 7 to Year 11, five lessons most days, and I'm still learning how to handle a bottom-set Year 10 group that has given up on maths. Evenings, I run a small online tutoring business, helping about twelve GCSE students on video calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does AI fit into all that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use it every day. I generate practice questions at three levels, get it to spot common mistakes in a pile of homework, and I use it to build worksheets for my tutoring clients. It's made the side business possible, honestly; I couldn't prepare for twelve students on top of a full timetable otherwise. My fiancée Lucia, who's an accountant, keeps the books for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool and that's all it ever needed to be. I'd post something on LinkedIn about using it well rather than chasing hype. In the staffroom I'd keep showing people the shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, that world is good for me. I've got a permanent job, a side business bringing in about £600 a month, and about five months saved. AI saves me time without threatening anything, so I keep the advantage. AI has made my tutoring business possible; I couldn't prepare for twelve students on top of a full timetable otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep growing the tutoring, maybe up to twenty students by next summer. I'd put half the tutoring money into an index fund every month. And Lucia and I would keep saving towards a deposit for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tutoring could grow to twenty. What limits it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, mostly. I can do evenings Monday to Thursday and Saturday mornings, but I don't want to burn out in my second year. If I grew past twenty, I'd hire a university student to take some of the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the school mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The head knows and doesn't mind, as long as I don't tutor our own students. I keep it to kids from other schools. It's a clean line and I stick to it.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, and that's enough.
I'd post on LinkedIn about **using it well** rather than chasing hype.
think: A **permanent job**, a side business and savings make this world good for me.
AI saves time **without threatening** anything I do.
do: Grow the tutoring to **twenty students** by next summer.
Put half the tutoring money into an **index fund**.
Keep saving for a **house deposit** with my fiancée.
S0.quote: AI has made my tutoring business possible; I couldn't prepare for twelve students on top of a full timetable otherwise.
fieldNote: He's an **everyday AI user** who turns it into side income.
His **side business** gives him a second income stream already.
He keeps a **clear ethical line** about not tutoring his own students.

steps.text: Grow online GCSE tutoring to twenty students by summer
Put half the tutoring income into an index fund
Save towards a house deposit with Lucia
Keep teaching maths at Northgate Academy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for teachers who adapt, and I'd say schools should let us use the tools freely. I'd probably run a session for staff. Online I'd write about how I use it, with examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot, but I'd watch two things. One, the academy chain might use AI to cut costs, maybe bigger maths classes with AI tutors for the weaker groups. Two, my tutoring business competes with AI tutoring apps that are cheaper than me, so I'd have to offer something they can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change the tutoring to small group sessions with a human coach, mostly focused on exam confidence and study habits, and use AI for the practice questions. I'd offer to lead AI training for the maths department. And I'd keep saving, but I'd also start a second investment account for the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit alert. Like I need to stay one step ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can you offer that the apps can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Accountability, mostly. A fifteen-year-old won't do practice questions because an app asks nicely, but they will if their tutor checks on Saturday. Parents pay for someone who knows their kid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Some of the older maths teachers don't use any of it, and if the chain starts measuring how fast we mark, they'll look slow. I'd help them, but I also think everyone has a responsibility to keep up.

say: I'd call it a **chance for teachers** who adapt.
I'd run a **staff session** and write about how I use AI.
think: The academy chain might use AI for **bigger maths classes**.
Cheaper **AI tutoring apps** compete with my side business.
do: Switch tutoring to **small groups** focused on exam confidence.
Offer to lead **AI training** for the maths department.
Open a second **investment account** for the business.
feel: **Calm** but **alert**, wanting to stay one step ahead.
S1.quote: A fifteen-year-old won't do practice questions because an app asks nicely, but they will if their tutor checks on Saturday.
fieldNote: He sees AI apps as **competitors** to his tutoring, not his teaching job.
His edge is **accountability**, something he thinks parents pay for.

steps.text: Turn tutoring into small groups focused on exam confidence
Lead AI training sessions for the maths department

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be calm and practical, and that schools should keep teachers but change how we work. I'd say families need to take more responsibility for kids' learning too. Online I'd be careful, because people would be angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the scary one for me. By 2028, AI can do almost any thinking work, so it can teach maths better than me and tutor better than me. My teaching job and my tutoring business are both in the firing line at the same moment. What's left is being a person kids respect, and I'm still learning that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change the tutoring into mentoring: study habits, motivation, careers advice for teenagers, before 2028. I'd move the index fund money into something steadier and build savings to eight months. And I'd talk to Lucia about whether we should still buy a house in 2027 or wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be up thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot date, around 2031, change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, because nearly all my work is thinking work. Maths, marking, tutoring, all of it goes in 2028. The robots matter more for people like my dad, who's a mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't blame the companies for making it. That's how markets work. I'd blame schools and governments if they didn't plan for kids, and I'd blame myself if I hadn't prepared.

say: I'd call for **calm and practical** change in schools.
I'd say **families** should take more responsibility for learning.
think: My **job and side business** are both at risk by 2028.
What's left is being a **person kids respect**.
do: Turn tutoring into **mentoring** for teenagers before 2028.
Move money to **steadier savings** and build eight months.
Rethink the **2027 house purchase** with my fiancée.
S2.quote: My teaching job and my tutoring business are both in the firing line at the same moment.
fieldNote: Both his incomes are **thinking work**, so 2028 is the date for him.
He blames **planners, not companies**, fitting his free-market outlook.
He'd move from tutoring to **mentoring** to stay useful.

steps.text: Rebuild tutoring as study-habit mentoring before 2028
Move the index fund into savings and reach eight months
Decide with Lucia whether to delay the 2027 house purchase

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years to prepare, so let's do it sensibly. I'd encourage colleagues to learn the tools now. I'd write a couple of posts about what I was changing in my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better. I'd have time to build the mentoring side properly, maybe take a coaching qualification. My maths teaching still goes by 2031, but I'd be in a better place by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a coaching qualification next year, around £1,500, paid from the tutoring money. I'd keep teaching and use AI heavily to save time. Lucia and I would still buy a house in 2027, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want room to move if things change. A smaller mortgage means if one of us loses work, we're not in trouble. Lucia's an accountant, and accountants are in the same boat as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn maths anyway, because it trains your thinking. And to learn how to work with people, because that's where jobs will be. I'd tell them that straight.

say: I'd say we have **a few years** to prepare sensibly.
I'd encourage colleagues to **learn the tools** now.
think: Five years lets me build the **mentoring side** properly.
My **maths teaching** still goes by 2031, though I'd be ready for it.
do: Keep teaching and use **AI heavily** to save time.
S3.quote: A smaller mortgage means if one of us loses work, we're not in trouble.
fieldNote: He'd shrink the **house plan** to keep flexibility.
His fiancée's **accountancy** job carries the same risk as his.
Five years gives him time to **qualify as a coach**.

steps.text: Take a coaching qualification for about £1,500
Use AI heavily for maths planning and marking
Buy a smaller house with Lucia in 2027

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great chance to get ahead, and that people should take it seriously now. I'd be optimistic in public, and in private too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'm thirty-seven when it lands. By then I'd want my own business, maybe a mentoring and tutoring centre with a few staff, and I'd have plenty of time to build it. My teaching job would change, but I'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching for five or six more years and grow the business slowly. I'd invest steadily, buy a house with Lucia, and get married in 2028. Around 2032, I'd decide whether to leave teaching for the business full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave teaching if my tutoring business was making more than my salary for two years in a row. I'm not reckless; I'd want proof first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, for everything except the human part. AI would make the practice questions, track progress and send reports to parents. My staff and I would do the mentoring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because both my incomes are thinking work and two years is short. What would help is less red tape on starting education businesses, and clear plans from schools about what teachers will do. Apprenticeships for teenagers would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: How teachers and families should work together. If AI teaches the facts, then parents and teachers have to work on character and habits together. That's where I'd put my energy.

headlineQuote: If AI teaches the facts, then parents and teachers have to work on character and habits together.
portrait: Omar is a second-year **maths teacher** at an academy who runs an online **tutoring business**.
He uses AI daily, has five months saved, and lives with his **accountant fiancée**.
He's **calm** in milder worlds but anxious in 2028, when both incomes are exposed.
He plans to build a **mentoring centre** and leave teaching only with proof it works.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **both his incomes** are thinking work.
whatWouldHelp: Clear plans from schools and **apprenticeships** for teenagers.
